731.quote_or_event: “In the night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was brought into the family of the Gñâtris their silver increased, their gold increased; their riches, corn, majesty, and kingdom increased; their army, train, treasure, storehouse, town, seraglio, subjects, and glory increased”
731.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra describes King Siddhartha's realm flourishing in grain, riches, stores and subjects from the moment the future Tirthankara entered the family, a sign of the merit attached to his presence.
731.tie_back: The Kural defines a true country by unfailing harvests, worthy people and lasting wealth; the Jain text presents the same marks of a flourishing realm as the result of a virtuous presence within it.
731.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
731._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (quoted up to the semicolon). It lists the same signs of prosperity, but as an auspicious omen in a story, not as a definition of a good country, and it says nothing about people of worth.

732.quote_or_event: “Knowing that the earth with its crops of rice and barley, with its gold and cattle, that all this put together will not satisfy one single man, one should practise austerities.”
732.explanation: King Nami, renouncing the kingdom of Mithila, answers Indra's call to enlarge his wealth by saying that even the whole earth's harvests and gold cannot satisfy one person's craving.
732.tie_back: The Kural praises a land so rich that others desire it; the Jain answer is that such desire for land is limitless, so the right response to a rich country is restraint, not covetousness.
732.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.49 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
732._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a contrast, not a parallel: Jainism names the same riches of the land but treats craving for them as bondage, so the fit is weak.

733.quote_or_event: “Karuna-Dana means gifts or offerings made out of compassion to any one who deserves it, being hungry, thirsty, diseased, distressed, disabled, helpless, or the like.”
733.explanation: Jain lay ethics urges the householder to give compassionate gifts (karuna-dana), commonly grouped as food, medicine, knowledge and protection from fear, to anyone in need, human or animal.
733.tie_back: Commentators read this Kural's sudden burden as people fleeing distress in other lands; the Jain duty of compassionate giving, including protection from fear, is the closest Jain counterpart to a land that can absorb such a burden.
733.source: 'Basic Positivity of Ahimsa', in The Jaina Path of Ahimsa (online book, jainworld.com)
733._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. Next-best only: this is a secondary summary of individual lay charity and has nothing to say about a land's capacity or about paying the ruler's dues.

734.quote_or_event: “Bhadrabahu, the last Srutakevali, predicted at Ujjain a twelve years drought and famine in the north, where upon the Jaina community migrated to the south under his leadership.”
734.explanation: Jain tradition, supported by Shravanabelagola inscriptions, holds that a twelve-year famine made the north unlivable for the monastic community, which moved south with Bhadrabahu (traditionally joined by Chandragupta Maurya).
734.tie_back: The Kural says a true country is untouched by crushing hunger; the Bhadrabahu story shows from the Jain side how famine strips a land of its worth, so that even the religious community has to leave it.
734.source: Jain Heritage Centres, 'Chandragiri' (Shravanabelagola), jainheritagecentres.com, summarising the Bhadrabahu tradition and Shravanabelagola inscriptions
734._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainheritagecentres.com, a secondary web source; the event is traditional and partly legendary. It covers famine only (not disease or enemies) and is a narrative, not a teaching about what makes a good land.

735.quote_or_event: “Punishing thieves and robbers, cut-purses and burglars, you should establish public safety; thus you will be a Kshattriya.” Nami answered: “Men frequently apply punishment wrongly: the innocent are put in prison, and the perpetrator of the crime is set at liberty.”
735.explanation: Indra, testing the renouncing King Nami, urges him to secure public safety by punishing criminals, and Nami replies that royal punishment often goes astray.
735.tie_back: The Kural wants a land free of internal enemies and murderous gangs; the Jain dialogue accepts that ideal of public safety, voiced by Indra, while doubting that a king's punishments can achieve it justly.
735.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.28 and 9.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
735._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best only: it names the threat of robbers and the duty of public safety, but the Jain voice is sceptical of the state's remedy and says nothing about factions.

736.quote_or_event: “The regions other than these are stable.”
736.explanation: Jain cosmology teaches that only Bharata and Airavata pass through cycles of rise and decline, while the other regions (such as Videha) stay in a stable condition; Pujyapada's commentary adds that they have no ascending or descending half-cycles of time.
736.tie_back: The Kural's best country is one that does not know ruin, or does not lose its richness even when harmed; Jain cosmology likewise imagines lands that never undergo decline.
736.source: Tattvartha Sutra 3.28, with Pujyapada's Sarvarthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
736._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The parallel is cosmological, not political: these regions are stable because of the structure of time, not because of resilience to harm by enemies.

737.quote_or_event: Indra: “Erect a wall, gates, and battlements; dig a moat; construct sataghnîs: then you will be a Kshattriya.” Nami: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable”
737.explanation: Urged to fortify Mithila with walls, moat and engines, the renouncing King Nami turns the fortress into a picture of the inner life, with faith, penance, self-control and patience as its walls and bolt.
737.tie_back: The Kural lists a strong fortress among the limbs of a country; the Jain text knows the same royal ideal of fortification but moves the real stronghold inside the soul.
737.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.18 and 9.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
737._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (verse 20 quoted only to its first clause). It matches the fortress only; the waters and hills of the Kural have no counterpart, and the Jain move is to spiritualise rather than endorse fortification.

738.quote_or_event: “May all subjects prosper, the king be strong and righteous, rains fall timely, diseases be eradicated, and may there be no fear of famine, theft, fire, or illness.”
738.explanation: The Shanti Path recited at the end of Digambara worship, addressed to Shantinatha, includes a prayer for the welfare of the whole realm: health, timely rain, plenty and security under a righteous king.
738.tie_back: The Kural names freedom from disease, wealth, harvests, happiness and security as a land's five ornaments; this Jain prayer asks for almost exactly the same goods for every country.
738.source: Shanti Path (Hindi Shanti Path of Digambara worship), verse 7, English rendering at frontdesk.co.in ('Shanti Path with Meaning', 2025)
738._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on frontdesk.co.in, a web translation of a liturgical prayer, not canonical scripture. It covers nearly all five of the Kural's ornaments; the Sanskrit counterpart (kṣemaṃ sarvaprajānāṃ...) was seen only in search results.

739.quote_or_event: “The others are called the ‘regions of enjoyment’–bhogabhūmi as the objects of enjoyment are provided by the ten kinds of desire-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa).”
739.explanation: Pujyapada contrasts the lands of labour (karmabhumi), where agriculture and the other occupations are needed, with the lands of enjoyment (bhogabhumi), where wish-fulfilling trees supply everything without effort.
739.tie_back: The Kural ranks highest the lands whose wealth comes without being sought; Jain cosmology has exactly such lands, though it also teaches that liberation can be won only in the lands of labour.
739.source: Tattvartha Sutra 3.37, with Pujyapada's Sarvarthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
739._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. A close match to wealth that comes unsought, but it is cosmology rather than advice on statecraft, and Jainism does not rank such lands highest spiritually.

740.quote_or_event: “During his reign he taught, for the benefit of the people, the seventy-two sciences, of which writing is the first, arithmetic the most important, and the knowledge of omens the last, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men.”
740.explanation: Rishabha, called 'First King' among his five names, is remembered as the ruler who gave his people the arts, sciences and occupations; Jacobi's note adds that the Kulakaras before him were the first kings and founders of families.
740.tie_back: The Kural says even a land with every excellence is fruitless without a fitting ruler; the Jain account of Rishabha likewise makes a wise king the one who turns a land's potential into a working society.
740.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha §§210-211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
740._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It shows the Jain ideal of a beneficial first king, but it does not say that a land is worthless without a fitting ruler; Rishabha in the end renounces kingship.
